items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long participial opener
items.passage: Excavating Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbor on Egypt’s Red Sea coast, archaeologist Pierre Tallet’s team uncovered the earliest surviving inscribed ______ by an inspector named Merer about 4,500 years ago, the logbooks document how his crew transported limestone from the Tura quarries to Giza.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “the earliest surviving inscribed papyri.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Written by an inspector named Merer about 4,500 years ago,” which describes its subject, “the logbooks,” and then gives the main verb “document.” Only a period separates these two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: “And” attaches the participial phrase to the first sentence, so the clause “the logbooks document how his crew transported limestone ...” is then joined to it with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “written by an inspector named Merer” reads as a description of the papyri, but the comma after “ago” then joins two independent clauses, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: The participial phrase opens the second independent clause, so the comma alone joins two independent clauses.

No logic-wrong distractor (the template's band-7 models have none).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before an appositive noun-phrase opener
items.passage: Male superb lyrebirds are renowned for imitating the songs of other species. In 2021, biologist Anastasia Dalziell and her collaborators documented a more elaborate ______ convincing acoustic illusion of a mixed-species flock mobbing a predator, this mimicry is performed by males exclusively during copulation or when a female attempts to depart.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2021 ... documented a more elaborate feat” is an independent clause. The noun phrase “A convincing acoustic illusion of a mixed-species flock mobbing a predator” renames the subject of the next clause, “this mimicry,” whose verb is “is performed.” A period is needed between the two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: The comma makes “a convincing acoustic illusion ...” look like an appositive for “feat,” but the clause “this mimicry is performed ...” then follows a comma alone, so two independent clauses are spliced.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the noun phrase runs into the first clause, and the independent clause “this mimicry is performed ...” is still joined with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: “And it is” turns the phrase into a second clause, but “this mimicry is performed ...” is a third independent clause attached with only a comma.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a prepositional opener
items.passage: Excavations directed by archaeologist Sun Zhouyong established that fortifications in China’s Shaanxi Province, long presumed to belong to the Great Wall, enclosed Shimao, a settlement built about 4,300 years ______ and around those fortifications, the team recovered some 70 stone reliefs depicting serpents, monsters, and half-human creatures.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a settlement built about 4,300 years ago.” The second sentence begins with the prepositional phrase “Within and around those fortifications,” followed by its subject and verb, “the team recovered.” A period correctly separates the two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: The phrase “within and around those fortifications” introduces the second independent clause, so the comma alone joins two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: Without a mark, “within and around those fortifications” attaches to “built about 4,300 years ago,” and the comma before “the team recovered” then splices two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: “And” links the prepositional phrase to the first sentence, but “the team recovered ...” is still an independent clause joined by only a comma.

items.subtype: Supplementary adverb closing clause 1 (L, however; R)
items.passage: Red-eyed treefrogs deposit their eggs on vegetation overhanging tropical ponds, where the embryos ordinarily hatch after six or seven days. That developmental timetable isn’t ______ as biologist Karen Warkentin has demonstrated, embryos in a clutch attacked by a snake can hatch prematurely, escaping their eggs within seconds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two independent clauses: “That developmental timetable isn’t fixed, however” and “as biologist ... within seconds.” “However” belongs to the first clause, signaling that it qualifies the usual six or seven days described in the previous sentence, so a comma sets it off and a semicolon joins the clauses. The second clause then explains why the timetable isn’t fixed.

A.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause presents premature hatching as a contrast to the timetable not being fixed, when it is the evidence for that claim.

C.why_wrong: Setting off “however” with commas leaves the two independent clauses joined by only a comma.

D.why_wrong: No mark separates “however” from the second clause, so the two independent clauses run together with no proper boundary.

sources.what: Karen Warkentin (Boston University biologist): red-eyed treefrog eggs laid on leaves over ponds hatch at six or seven days; embryos hatch early when a snake bites the clutch but not in response to rain
startled embryos escape the egg within seconds

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening clause 2 (L; rather, R)
items.passage: English speakers characteristically gesture forward when referring to the future and backward for the past. The Yupno of Papua New Guinea don’t anchor temporal concepts to the body in this ______ as cognitive scientist Rafael Núñez and colleagues reported in 2012, they gesture uphill for the future and downhill for the past.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence contains two independent clauses: “The Yupno ... don’t anchor temporal concepts to the body in this way” and “they gesture uphill for the future and downhill for the past.” A semicolon joins them, and “rather,” followed by a comma, introduces the second clause, which says what the Yupno do instead.

A.why_wrong: No punctuation separates the first independent clause from the second, which begins after “as ... reported in 2012.”

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the independent clause ending with “this way” to the independent clause “they gesture uphill ....”

C.why_wrong: Setting off “rather” with commas still leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that specifies it
items.passage: Land snails crawl so slowly that their dispersal across islands has long puzzled biologists. In 2011, ecologist Shinichiro Wada and colleagues proposed an improbable means of ______ digestive tracts of birds such as the Japanese white-eye, through which roughly 15 percent of the minuscule snails they fed to captive birds passed alive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “In 2011, ecologist ... proposed an improbable means of transport” is complete, and what follows is a noun phrase that identifies that means of transport. A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation after a complete clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “the digestive tracts of birds ...” is a noun phrase; its verb “passed” belongs to a relative clause.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “The digestive tracts of birds ... passed alive” a sentence fragment: the only verb sits inside the relative clause “through which ...”.

D.recipe: added word creates the error (comma splice)
D.why_wrong: “It was” turns the phrase into an independent clause, which is then joined to the first clause with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: The period turns “The side in contact with water” into a sentence fragment.

items.subtype: Restrictive descriptor plus name, followed by the verb and an integrated quotation

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: Mexican novelist Yuri Herrera’s border trilogy, translated by Lisa Dillman, comprises Kingdom Cons, in which a balladeer joins the court of a drug lord known as the ______ Preceding the End of the World, which follows a young woman’s clandestine border crossing; and The Transmigration of Bodies, set during an epidemic.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three novels, and each item contains its own comma before a description. When items in a series contain commas, semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon before “and The Transmigration of Bodies” shows. A semicolon is therefore needed between the first item and the second, “Signs Preceding the End of the World.”

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the first item runs straight into the second, so “the King Signs Preceding the End of the World” reads as a single confused phrase.

items.subtype: Comma pair around a supplementary adverb before a participial phrase (no second clause)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a participial opener
items.passage: Pumpkin toadlets, miniature frogs endemic to Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, leap readily but frequently tumble midair and crash on ______ the toadlets’ inner ears, a team led by biologist Richard Essner determined that the semicircular canals, which detect rotation, are too small to function reliably.

A.why_wrong: The participial phrase belongs to the second independent clause, so the comma alone joins two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and the comma after “ears” then joins “a team ... determined” to the first clause.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening clause 2 (L; however, R)

items.subtype: Supplementary adverb closing clause 1 (L, though; R)
items.passage: A mammal’s skull ordinarily stays the same size once the animal reaches maturity. The common shrew, an insectivore of Europe and northern Asia, is a striking ______ each autumn its skull and brain shrink before partially regrowing in spring, a cycle that may reduce its metabolic demands in winter.

A.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “though,” the two independent clauses are joined with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: “Though” would then introduce “each autumn its skull and brain shrink ...” as a concession, but the shrinking is the reason the shrew is an exception, not something that works against it.

C.why_wrong: “Though” would make the words after the semicolon a dependent clause, which cannot stand on its own after a semicolon.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: Researchers at Newcastle University investigated whether praying mantises, like humans, perceive depth by comparing the slightly different images from their two eyes. The team fitted mantises with miniature 3D glasses and projected simulated prey onto a ______ the insects struck only when the stereoscopic illusion placed the prey within reach.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The team fitted mantises with miniature 3D glasses and projected simulated prey onto a screen” and “the insects struck only when ...” are both independent clauses. A comma and the coordinating conjunction “and” join them.

A.why_wrong: When “and” joins two independent clauses of this length, a comma is needed before it.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: science (insect vision). Medium: clause 1 itself contains a compound verb joined by “and,” so the student must see that “the insects struck” starts a new clause.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: The Garima Gospels, two illuminated manuscripts kept at a monastery in northern Ethiopia, were long assumed to date from around the eleventh ______ radiocarbon dating of their pages later indicated that they were made between the fourth and seventh centuries, placing them among the oldest illustrated Christian books in existence.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The Garima Gospels ... were long assumed to date from around the eleventh century” and “radiocarbon dating of their pages later indicated ...” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “but” joins them and signals the contrast between the old assumption and the new dates.

A.why_wrong: A comma is needed before “but” when it joins two independent clauses this long.

C.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “but”; it separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: history (manuscripts, Ethiopia). Medium: 1.31-style option set with `, but,` in place of the plain splice.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Archaeologists long wondered what tall cylindrical jars from Pueblo Bonito, a great house in New Mexico’s Chaco Canyon, had held. In 2009, anthropologist Patricia Crown found that residue on fragments of the jars contained theobromine, a compound present in ______ then, no evidence of chocolate drinking had turned up north of Mexico.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence about Crown’s finding ends with “a compound present in cacao.” “Until then” is a short introductory phrase that opens the next independent clause, whose subject is “no evidence.” A period separates the two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: The comma joins two independent clauses, with “until then” attached to the first.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “until then” seems to modify “cacao,” and the two independent clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: “And” without a comma does not properly join two independent clauses, and it leaves “until then” unclear.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology of the US Southwest). Medium: 2-word opener after the period, as in 2.7 and 2.9.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: The twelfth-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Tufayl explored the capacities of unaided human reason in his philosophical novel Hayy ibn ______ a boy who, raised by a gazelle on an uninhabited island, deduces the principles of natural science and philosophy entirely on his own.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with the title “Hayy ibn Yaqzan.” The participial phrase “imagining a boy who ...” is a supplementary element describing how Ibn Tufayl explored human reason, so a comma separates it from the main clause.

B.why_wrong: The words after the semicolon have no subject or finite verb of their own, so they cannot stand as an independent clause.

C.why_wrong: “Imagining a boy who ...” has no main verb, so it cannot be a sentence.

D.why_wrong: “And” suggests that a second action parallel to “explored” follows, but “imagining ...” is a participial phrase, not a verb that can share the subject “Ibn Tufayl.”

items.notes: Subject: literature and philosophy. Medium: trailing -ing phrase after a long main clause, as in 2.26; the phrase holds its own comma-set interrupter.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory participial phrase
items.passage: Paradise tree snakes of Southeast Asia glide between treetops by flattening their bodies. Recording the snakes with motion-capture cameras as they launched from a platform inside a four-story ______ team led by biologist Jake Socha determined that the snakes’ midair undulations prevent them from tumbling.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Recording the snakes ... inside a four-story arena” is an introductory participial phrase, not a complete sentence. A comma separates it from the main clause that follows, whose subject is “a team led by biologist Jake Socha” and whose verb is “determined.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the introductory phrase has no subject or main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period turns the introductory phrase into a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: “And” would join the introductory phrase to the main clause as if both were clauses, but the phrase has no subject or main verb.

items.notes: Subject: science (biomechanics). Medium: a 16-word introductory phrase with an embedded as-clause, so the main subject is far from the start of the sentence.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: In the ultimatum game, one participant proposes how to divide a sum of money, and a second participant accepts the proposal or rejects it, leaving both empty-handed. The Machiguenga horticulturalists whom anthropologist Joseph Henrich recruited to play the game in the Peruvian ______ made low offers, yet their counterparts seldom rejected them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “The Machiguenga horticulturalists whom anthropologist Joseph Henrich recruited to play the game in the Peruvian Amazon,” and its verb is “made.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject from its verb, “made.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; the words before it are only the subject.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the words before it have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics, anthropology). Medium: 16-word subject with a relative clause and a place phrase before the verb, as in 2.3.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: German-born Venezuelan artist Gego transformed the line into a three-dimensional presence in series such as Reticulárea, an immersive web of interconnected wire first exhibited in Caracas in ______ Troncos, cylindrical columns built from metal rods; and Dibujos sin papel (Drawings without Paper), constructions in which wire substitutes for pencil lines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three series, each followed by a description set off by a comma. Because the items contain commas, semicolons separate them, as the semicolon before “and Dibujos sin papel” shows. A semicolon is needed after “1969” to end the first item.

A.why_wrong: A comma here would not match the semicolon used between the second and third items, so the items would be hard to tell apart.

C.why_wrong: A colon would present “Troncos” as an explanation of the first item rather than as the next item in the list.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the first item runs directly into the second.

items.notes: Subject: arts (sculpture). Medium: single-slot complex series with the blank closing item 1, as in 2.16.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: The Dunhuang Star Chart, a paper scroll produced in China during the Tang dynasty, is the oldest complete star atlas known from any civilization. Depicting more than 1,300 stars, it was discovered in 1900 among thousands ______ manuscripts concealed inside a Buddhist cave temple.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Of manuscripts” is a prepositional phrase: “manuscripts” is the object of the preposition “of.” No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; it cannot separate a preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “of” from its object.

D.why_wrong: The dash has no role here and separates the preposition from its object.

items.notes: Subject: history (Chinese astronomy, Mogao Caves). Easy: preposition-object boundary, four distinct marks.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Ghanaian philosopher Kwasi Wiredu called for the “conceptual decolonization” of African thought. He urged African philosophers to ______ concepts such as “truth” and “mind,” which had reached them through colonial education, by asking whether those concepts made sense in African languages such as his native Akan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Concepts such as ‘truth’ and ‘mind’” is the direct object of the verb “reexamine.” No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; “He urged African philosophers to reexamine” is incomplete without its object.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the verb from its object.

D.why_wrong: The dash separates the verb from its object and has no partner.

items.notes: Subject: philosophy. Easy: verb-object boundary as in 1.15 and 1.16.

items.subtype: Direct question: inverted word order and a question mark
items.passage: In 2019, researchers reported that Atlantic puffins in Wales and Iceland had been filmed scratching their bodies with small sticks, the first documented instance of tool use among seabirds. The discovery raised a new question: How ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: did the puffins learn this behavior.
did the puffins learn this behavior?
items.explanation: After the colon, “How” begins a direct question, so the helping verb “did” comes before the subject (“did the puffins learn”) and the sentence ends with a question mark.

A.why_wrong: A direct question beginning with “How” needs the helping verb before the subject, not statement word order.

B.recipe: question errors (direct question ends with a period)
B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question ends with a question mark.

C.recipe: question errors (statement order and a period)
C.why_wrong: This is neither a correctly formed question nor a complete statement: “How the puffins learned this behavior” cannot stand as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal behavior). Easy: direct question after a colon, as in 1.18 (b1 used an embedded why-question).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: Biologists in Japan have found that the sea slug Elysia marginata can detach its head from its body at the ______ the head subsequently regenerates an entirely new body, heart included, within approximately three weeks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Biologists in Japan have found that the sea slug ... can detach its head from its body at the neck” and “the head subsequently regenerates an entirely new body ...” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “and” joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma is needed before “and” when it joins two independent clauses of this length.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “and”; it separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: science (regeneration). Easy: clause 2 opens with its subject right after the blank.

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series
items.passage: Hogeweyk, a gated village that opened in 2009 in Weesp, the Netherlands, was designed specifically for residents with advanced dementia. They occupy small shared households and can wander freely through streets and courtyards that contain a ______ a restaurant, and a theater.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A supermarket,” “a restaurant,” and “a theater” are three items in a simple series. A comma separates the first item from the second, matching the comma after “restaurant.”

A.why_wrong: Semicolons separate list items only when the items contain commas; these do not.

B.why_wrong: A colon would present the rest of the list as an explanation of “a supermarket.”

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first two items of the series run together.

items.notes: Subject: social science (elder care, urban design). Easy: blank after item 1 of three, as in 1.25 and 1.12, so the serial-comma question never arises.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing such as phrase
items.passage: Nüshu, a script once used exclusively by women, developed over centuries in Jiangyong County in China’s Hunan Province. Women used Nüshu in letters and songs and wrote or embroidered its characters on everyday objects exchanged between sworn sisters or between mothers and ______ as fans and handkerchiefs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Such as fans and handkerchiefs” gives examples of the “everyday objects” mentioned earlier, not of daughters, so it is a supplementary phrase at the end of the sentence and is set off with a comma.

A.why_wrong: The words after the semicolon are a phrase, not an independent clause.

B.why_wrong: “Such as fans and handkerchiefs” has no subject or verb and cannot stand as a sentence.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the examples seem to describe “daughters” rather than the objects.

items.notes: Subject: language and writing systems. Easy: such-as tail whose examples belong to a noun earlier in the sentence, as in 1.11, so the no-comma version misreads.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around a which clause
items.passage: In 2021, primatologists reported that two wild female bonobos had adopted infants from neighboring communities. The adoptions, which occurred at Wamba, a research site in the Democratic Republic of the ______ were the first such cases documented among wild great apes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “adoptions” opens the supplementary clause “which occurred at Wamba, a research site in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.” A comma after “Congo” closes it before the verb “were.”

B.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the supplementary clause runs into the main verb “were.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon would separate the subject “The adoptions” from its verb “were.”

D.why_wrong: “And” makes “were the first such cases” part of the which clause, so the sentence has no main verb for “The adoptions.”

items.notes: Subject: science (primatology). Easy: closing comma of a which clause that holds an appositive, partner 14 words back, as in 1.10.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a noun-phrase opener
items.passage: In 1938, a man excavating a cistern in the town of Igbo-Ukwu in southeastern Nigeria encountered a cache of buried ______ ornamented vessels, ceremonial altar stands, and pendants cast around the ninth century CE, the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are among the oldest surviving metal castings from West Africa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1938 ... encountered a cache of buried objects” is a complete sentence. The noun phrase “Intricately ornamented vessels, ceremonial altar stands, and pendants cast around the ninth century CE” describes the subject of the next sentence, “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes,” which has its own verb, “are.” A period is needed between the two independent clauses.

A.recipe: comma splice (opener read as an appositive to clause 1)
A.why_wrong: The comma makes the list look like a description of “objects,” but “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “That were” attaches the noun phrase to the first clause, which still leaves “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are ...” joined to it with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “objects intricately ornamented vessels” runs the two clauses together, and the comma before “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes” then splices them.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (West African bronze casting). Band 7: a 14-word noun-phrase opener with an internal series that reads as an appositive to clause 1's last noun until “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are” arrives 15 words after the blank (0fa289a7 / 940ff6f7 shape).

band7.why: 0fa289a7 / 940ff6f7 shape with the a872c60a menu (period key, splice, glued, added 'that were'): a 14-word noun-phrase opener with an internal series reads as an appositive to 'objects' until 'the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are' arrives 15 words after the blank; one 46-word run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a Because-clause opener
items.passage: Unlike conventional white paint, which reflects only 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight, the paint that engineer Xiulin Ruan and his colleagues unveiled in 2021 stays cool even under a midday ______ the paint reflects roughly 98 percent of sunlight while radiating heat as infrared light, a coated surface can remain cooler than the surrounding air.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Unlike conventional white paint ... under a midday sun” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the dependent clause “Because the paint reflects ... infrared light,” and its main clause is “a coated surface can remain cooler than the surrounding air.” A period is needed between the two sentences.

A.recipe: comma splice (subordinate clause read as part of clause 1)
A.why_wrong: The “because” clause seems to explain the first clause, but “a coated surface can remain cooler” is a second independent clause, so the sentence joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

B.recipe: comma splice (subordinate clause glued to clause 1)
B.why_wrong: Without punctuation the “because” clause attaches to the first clause, and the comma after “light” then joins “a coated surface can remain cooler ...” to it, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “That” starts a relative clause that never gets a verb of its own, so the sentence breaks down; it also leaves the two main clauses joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (radiative cooling paint). Band 7: clause 2 opens with a subordinator (615f001e move), so the comma and no-mark versions read naturally until the main clause's subject appears about 15 words later. No semicolon or colon option: both would be acceptable before a because-clause opener.

band7.why: 615f001e move: clause 2 opens with 'Because', so the comma and no-mark versions read as a natural because-clause on clause 1 until 'a coated surface' arrives 15 words after the blank. 56-word run, but every part does work (the 80 to 90 percent baseline gives '98 percent' its point; the infrared radiation is what makes 'cooler than the surrounding air' true), so not trimmed.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a gerund subject
items.passage: Hoping to curb dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, researchers released mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia, a bacterium that prevents the virus from replicating, across half of 24 designated neighborhoods in Yogyakarta, ______ Wolbachia into the local mosquito population reduced dengue incidence there by roughly 77 percent, the team reported in 2021.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Hoping to curb dengue ... in Yogyakarta, Indonesia” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has the gerund phrase “Introducing Wolbachia into the local mosquito population” as its subject and “reduced” as its verb. A period is needed to separate the two independent clauses.

B.recipe: comma splice (gerund subject read as a participial phrase)
B.why_wrong: The comma makes “introducing ...” look like a modifier of the first clause, but it is the subject of “reduced,” so two independent clauses are joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the first clause runs straight into the second clause's subject, “Introducing Wolbachia ...,” which has the verb “reduced.”

D.why_wrong: “By” turns the subject into a phrase about how the mosquitoes were released, so the verb “reduced” is left with no subject.

items.notes: Subject: science (public health, mosquito-borne disease). Band 6: gerund subject of clause 2 (73a6603c shape); the verb that resolves it comes 7 words after the blank, and the city-country comma (Yogyakarta, Indonesia,) makes the comma option look natural.

band7.why: 73a6603c shape: gerund subject resolved by 'reduced' 7 words after the blank; the city-country comma makes B look natural. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, colon before an explanation
items.passage: Visitors to an art gallery typically expect simply to contemplate whatever is on display. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s 1992 exhibition Untitled (Free) asked its visitors to do more than ______ he converted the New York gallery’s back office into a makeshift kitchen and invited them to linger, eat the curry he prepared, and converse with strangers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The adverb “however” belongs to the first clause: the exhibition asking visitors to do more than look contrasts with the previous sentence, in which visitors expect only to contemplate what is displayed. The comma sets “however” off from that clause, and the colon introduces the second clause, which explains what more the exhibition asked of them.

A.why_wrong: A comma after “however” cannot join the two independent clauses “Thai artist ... however” and “he converted ... with strangers.”

B.why_wrong: Nothing marks the boundary after “however,” so the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause signals that converting the office into a kitchen and inviting visitors to eat and talk contrasts with asking them to do more than look, but it is exactly the “more” that the first clause describes.

items.notes: Subject: arts (relational art, 1992 gallery show). Band 7: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; colon variant (84658166); the strongest distractor is the textbook `; however,` placement, wrong only by meaning. No `however;` option, since a semicolon after however would also be acceptable.

band7.why: 84658166 / c15069eb menu: ', however:' closes clause 1 and answers sentence 1 (visitors expect only to contemplate); D's textbook '; however,' is wrong only by meaning, since the kitchen is the 'more' that clause 1 announces, not a contrast with it. No ', however;' option, which would also be acceptable.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, period before the next sentence

The poems are rarely as innocent as they seem, ______ frequently conceal a second, mischievous meaning that ridicules the pompous scholars and monks of her era.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

A.why_wrong: “However” is not a conjunction, so a comma after it joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation after “however.”

D.recipe: conjunction without comma, adverb glued to the conjunction
D.why_wrong: “But” needs a comma before it to join these long clauses, and it signals a second contrast that the text does not contain.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Vietnamese poetry, double meanings). Band 6: the period-after-adverb shape of 2bb7416a (not used in b1 or b2); the decision rests on reading “however” as part of clause 1.

band7.why: 2bb7416a menu ('however. They' key, splice, fused, 'however but'): the decision is reading 'however' as part of clause 1, with no logic-wrong option. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: No comma before a restrictive that-clause
items.passage: Whereas many Western writing guides treat conflict as the engine of every plot, kishōtenketsu is a four-part model for ______ writers in China, Japan, and Korea have long employed: an introduction, a development, an apparently unrelated twist, and a conclusion that reconciles the preceding parts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That many writers in China, Japan, and Korea have long employed” is a restrictive clause: it identifies which model for storytelling the text means. No punctuation goes between “storytelling” and “that,” and the colon after “employed” then introduces the four parts.

A.why_wrong: A comma is not used before “that” when it introduces a clause essential to the noun it modifies.

B.why_wrong: “Many writers ... have long employed” is not a complete sentence, because the verb “employed” still needs its object. A colon can’t follow it, and a colon can’t separate a verb from its object, so the list after the colon can’t complete it.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “many writers ... have long employed” lacks the object of “employed,” and the colon after it can’t supply one, since a colon can’t separate a verb from its object.

items.notes: Subject: literature (narrative structure). Band 6: restrictive that-clause with the omitted-object trap of 5ef9fc48.

fixes: B and D why_wrong: name the rule (a colon can't follow an incomplete clause or separate a verb from its object), since the list after the colon looks like an object

band7.why: 5ef9fc48 menu and move: restrictive that-clause whose verb lacks an object, so the period and semicolon options leave no clause; local. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (word as word) followed by a nonrestrictive which-clause

B.why_wrong: The comma separates “word” from the word it names, and no comma sets off the which-clause.

items.passage: Mudskippers are amphibious fish that spend much of their lives out of water, perched on rocks and mangrove roots. They hop across intertidal mudflats on their muscular front ______ can absorb oxygen through their skin and the lining of their mouths, provided that both stay moist.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “They hop across intertidal mudflats on their muscular front fins” is a complete sentence, and so is “They can absorb oxygen through their skin ....” A period correctly separates the two.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation.

C.why_wrong: “And” without a comma does not properly join two independent clauses this long.
